uncited: Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) and its variants synthesize novel views of 3D scenes from a sparse set of posed 2D images by learning a continuous function that maps spatial coordinates and viewing directions to volume density and emitted color [S3, S4, unofficial].

What sets the family apart from explicit grid-based siblings like [Explicit Radiance Fields](806-explicit-radiance-fields.md) and [Plenoxels](1501-plenoxels.md) is the use of neural networks (typically MLPs) to represent the scene implicitly, allowing for high-fidelity reconstruction of complex geometry and view-dependent appearance without explicit mesh or voxel structures [S2, S3, unofficial].
The core mechanism involves differentiable volume rendering.
A ray $\mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}$ is cast from the camera through each pixel.
For each sample, a scene representation predicts volume density $\sigma_i$ and color $\mathbf{c}_i$.

where $\alpha_i = 1 - \exp(-\sigma_i \delta_i)$ is the opacity of the sample, $\delta_i$ is the distance to the next sample, and $T_i = \prod_{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alpha_j)$ is the accumulated transmittance [S5, S6, unofficial].
The scene is optimized by minimizing the Mean Squared Error (MSE) between the rendered color $\hat{C}$ and the ground truth image color $C$ [S2, S4, unofficial].
It addressed the limitations of previous implicit representations by introducing hierarchical sampling and view-dependent color encoding.
